newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban seen drawing Dostum into Afghan war.
newsitem.headline: Taleban seen drawing Dostum into Afghan war.

text.p: The Afghan Taleban, hurling bombs and insults across the battlefield north of Kabul and opening a new front in the northwest, have thrown down the gauntlet to the country's most powerful army, Afghan watchers said on Saturday.
"They are displaying great confidence, but unless they are much stronger than we think they are, they are taking a considerable risk," said one.
The purist Islamic militia, a month after taking Kabul, effectively declared dead on Friday ceasefire talks with northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.
It denounced him as a "former communist and criminal", then opened up a new front by attacking Dostum in Badghis in the northwest, one of six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces Dostum controlled.

"This may have been the excuse Dostum was waiting for," said another Afghan watcher. "They are attacking him where he is strong before ceasefire talks are officially declared a failure and Dostum can portray himself as the victim."
"They have opened up a new front at a time the main front is in a stalemate and, if Dostum can hit back as hard as we think he can, the Taleban may have given him a strategic opening."
The Uzbek leader sent tanks, artillery and men two weeks ago to join the front lines of his once-again ally, former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, north of Kabul.

Although he seems to have backed Masood's efforts to break through Taleban lines on the plain with artillery, it is far from clear that Dostum has committed his ground troops, the Afghan watchers said.
"If he does, then the Taleban are going to have serious difficulty holding their line," one said.

The fighting north of Kabul has been deadlocked for nearly a week, with repeated Masood attempts to break through Taleban lines on a series of hills straggling across the plain 25-30 km (15-18 miles) north of Kabul beaten back.
The Afghan watchers said Masood was in difficulty, having blocked the entrance to his Panjsher Valley stronghold further north as he retreated from Kabul.
"He is having a hard time getting his equipment, especially ammunition which he is having to get out by donkey, out of the valley," said one reliable source.

The source said a series of Taleban bombing raids on Friday was aimed at the valley entrance, where Masood was using bulldozers in an attempt to clear the landslides he created to prevent the Taleban getting in nearly a month ago.
"The Taleban up on the front line are showing great confidence after stopping Masood's advances, but that could erode very quickly if Dostum steps in with force," an Afghan watcher said.

Dostum, a former communist general who switched sides just before mujahidden guerrillas toppled a Moscow-backed government in 1992, is widely regarded as commanding Afghanistan's most powerful fighting force. He also has a small air force.
The Afghan watchers said Dostum had enough men and equipment to fight on the fronts north of Kabul and in Badghis.
"If he commits them, and it is still an 'if' because Dostum's record is one of sending his forces into action only when he has to, then the Taleban could be in trouble," said one.

He said if Dostum rolled back the Taleban in Badghis, then the western city of Herat became vulnerable. Herat has a large population of ethnic Tajiks, Masood's people, and the largely Pashtun Taleban and thought to be unpopular there.

"If Herat falls, then Kandahar becomes vulnerable," one military analyst said of the southern city that is the Taleban headquarters. "It only took the Taleban four days to get from Kandahar to Herat, so the opposite must be possible."
"What we don't know is just how many men the Taleban have and to what point they will go on fighting," he said.
"So we have two big questions; can the Taleban hold two fronts and will Dostum commit himself all the way? We may know the answers soon."
